【turn589888654news21】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 10 months ago; Crawled: yesterday; Content type: text/html; 
According to the North Carolina State Veterinary Hospital, cats with large cell GI lymphoma receiving CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone) therapy have a prognosis of 6 to 9 months.^{2} Meanwhile, cats with small cell GI lymphoma have a longer prognosis of typically 2 to 3 years or more, but chronic treatment with oral medications is required.^{2}

According to Texas A&M University, the GI tract is home to a high number of lymphocytes, making it a common site of lymphoma in feline patients.^{1} In fact, small cell GI lymphoma is the most common type of lymphoma in cats^{3} and is the most frequently diagnosed digestive tract cancer in these animals.^{1}

“Small cell GI lymphoma is the most common cancer of a cat’s digestive system and a highly prevalent feline cancer overall,” Regina Hayburn, DVM, DACVIM (Oncology), a clinical assistant professor of medical oncology at Texas A&M’s Department of Small Animal Clinical Sciences, said in the Texas A&M report.^{1} “It can form anywhere along the digestive tract, including the stomach, small intestine, or colon.”

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and small cell GI lymphoma are thought to be closely related, representing different stages of the same underlying process. Veterinary researchers have found that GI inflammatory lesions, a major characteristic of IBD, often coexist with small cell GI lymphoma.^{4} This overlap has led to the proposition that chronic inflammatory lesions might progress to lymphoma over time.^{4} As such, many researchers and veterinarians have described small cell GI lymphoma as being a “spectrum of disease” with IBD.^{1,4}

“Because of the impaired motility and absorption, chronic vomiting and diarrhea are common, along with weight loss and decreased appetite, although some cats maintain a normal or even increased appetite in early stages,” Hayburn said in the Texas A&M report.^{1} “As the disease progresses, cats often stop eating, vomit more frequently, and become increasingly lethargic and generally unwell due to chronic illness and weight loss.” Bloody stools may also be a sign of small cell GI lymphoma and IBD.

## Study title

A Pilot Study Evaluating PARP Inhibition in Combination with NSAID Therapy in Cats with Mammary Carcinoma

## Purpose of study

Feline mammary carcinoma (FMC) is an aggressive cancer with limited effective treatment options and poor long-term outcomes. In addition to exhibiting similar biologic behavior, there is a growing body of evidence indicating that many FMCs display molecular characteristics similar to triple-negative (TNBC) and basal-like subtypes of human breast cancer. These aggressive forms of human breast cancer have shown encouraging responses to olaparib, an oral Poly (ADP) ribose polymerase inhibitor. This medication alters DNA repair pathways, which are thought to be a major contributor to resistance to traditional chemotherapy. Olaparib is well-tolerated in humans, and early data obtained by researchers at the University of Illinois suggests that it is well-tolerated and shows clinical activity in cats with cancer.

This is a pilot study that combines olaparib and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medication (meloxicam) for treatment of FMC. Meloxicam is used as a pain medication, and it has direct anti-cancer effects for many carcinomas.

The latest updates relating to animal care establishments and platforms.

In Sacramento, California, the University of California, Davis (UC Davis) has launched the Translational Brain Tumor Center, a new research initiative connecting its veterinary and human medicine programs to advance brain cancer treatments across species. Meanwhile, in Logan, Utah, Purina Pro Plan Veterinary has opened a student wellness center at Utah State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine, the latest initiative under its Pro Plan Veterinary Support Mission. And in Dallas, Texas, CityVet has opened CityVet Bishop Arts under a local veterinarian.

## UC Davis opens center focused on brain tumors in people and pets

The UC Davis Translational Brain Tumor Center connects researchers and clinicians from the UC Davis Weill School of Veterinary Medicine and UC Davis Health to study brain cancers across species. The center launches with two active National Cancer Institute–funded clinical trials recruiting dogs diagnosed with or suspected of having glioma: the CARE trial and the PRISM trial. The CARE trial is evaluating an experimental drug intended to make glioma cells more vulnerable to radiation therapy, while the PRISM trial tracks tumor progression and combines clinical data with genetic and immune profiling to identify subtypes that may support more personalized treatment.

Companion dogs can develop brain tumors that share characteristics with human cancers—including genetic changes, neurological symptoms, patterns of growth, and treatment resistance—making them a relevant population for studying naturally occurring disease under clinical conditions.

The center supports advanced imaging, molecular research, biobanking, multidisciplinary clinical care, and education in comparative neuro-oncology.

The center is being led by Christine Toedebusch, DVM, PhD, DACVIM (Neurology), a veterinary clinician-scientist specializing in neurology and comparative neuro-oncology. “We have remarkable expertise across UC Davis. The greatest advances will come from connecting that expertise around shared questions,” Toedebusch said in a university report.^{1} “The center creates a structure for investigators and clinicians to work together from the beginning rather than waiting until a discovery is ready to be handed from one field to another.”

## Purina Pro Plan announces veterinary student wellness center at Utah State University in Logan, Utah

Purina Pro Plan Veterinary has opened the Purina Pro Plan Wellness Center at Utah State University’s (USU) College of Veterinary Medicine, providing students with dedicated space for one-on-one sessions with wellness specialists and areas for meditation and mindfulness practice. The opening comes as USU continues to build its 4-year Doctor of Veterinary Medicine program, which welcomed its inaugural class of 39 students in August 2025 and its second class of 77 students this fall.

“The Purina Pro Plan Wellness Center represents our commitment to making wellbeing an integral part of veterinary education,” said Michael Bishop, director of student affairs for USU’s College of Veterinary Medicine, in a news release.^{2}

"The GluCurve Pet CGM is designed to help animal health professionals manage diabetes in new and innovative ways."

According to studies^{1,2}, 1 in 300 dogs and 1 in 175 cats have diabetes and until now, regulating blood sugar using human CGMs off label could be a real challenge for pet parents and veterinarians. The GluCurve is the first and only continuous glucose monitoring system built specifically for veterinary use on cats and dogs. A pet-friendly CGM sensor is painlessly and effortlessly attached to the pet, providing blood sugar levels every minute for up to 14 days. Pet owners can view the blood sugar readings live on the GluCurve Pet CGM app, while veterinarians use a custom-built veterinary web portal designed to make managing blood sugar easier and more effective to optimize glucose regulation and improve health outcomes.

Sales of the GluCurve Pet CGM in the United States are expected to commence in December of 2026.

# Compressed 2-dose melarsomine protocol is safe and effective in shelter dogs with heartworm, JAVMA trial finds

Author(s)Justin Louis, Content Producer

Fact checked by: Yasmeen Qahwash

A randomized trial of 168 shelter dogs found that a shorter, 2-injection heartworm treatment was safe and effective. Every dog survived treatment, and most tested negative afterward.

A shortened heartworm treatment using 2 injections of melarsomine was safe and effective in shelter dogs with subclinical to moderate disease, according to a randomized clinical trial published in the Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association.^{1} All 168 dogs in the study survived treatment, and none required intensive management or hospitalization for complications.

Researchers from Toronto Humane Society, the University of Florida Shelter Medicine Program, Lucky Dog Animal Rescue, and EveryPet compared compressed 2-dose and 3-dose melarsomine protocols. Each protocol was paired with the adjunctive therapies now standard in heartworm treatment: sustained-release moxidectin, doxycycline, and prednisone.^{1} The study authors described the trial as the largest randomized controlled clinical trial in the heartworm literature. PetSmart Charities funded the research.^{1}

The American Heartworm Society (AHS) has recommended a 3-dose melarsomine protocol for all dogs, regardless of clinical status, since 2005.^{1} According to the study authors, the AHS recommendation followed early research in which melarsomine was the sole therapeutic agent. In the early studies, the 3-dose protocol was more effective than the 2-dose protocol. It also carried lower risks of complications and death in more severe cases. Since then, a macrocyclic lactone heartworm preventive, a 28-day course of doxycycline, and prednisone have become standard components of treatment guidelines. Aside from a recent retrospective study by the same research group, no studies had compared 2-dose and 3-dose melarsomine, according to the authors.^{1}

The trial ran from April 2024 to December 2025 at the Lucky Dog Animal Rescue campus in Florence, South Carolina.^{1} Dogs at least 12 months old with class 1 or class 2 heartworm disease were randomly assigned to a treatment group. Of 170 dogs enrolled, 168 remained in the study after 2 exclusions: 85 in the 2-dose group and 83 in the 3-dose group. Dogs with more severe heartworm disease were not enrolled.

# First Patient Dosed in VIR-5500 T-Cell Engager Trial in Metastatic Prostate Cancer

Author(s)Tony Berberabe, MPH

Fact checked by: Jonah Feldman

The first patient has been dosed in a phase 1 trial (NCT05997615) of VIR-5500, a dual-masked PSMA-targeting T-cell engager for metastatic prostate cancer.

The first patient has been dosed in 1 of 3 expansion cohorts in the phase 1 trial (NCT05997615) evaluating VIR-5500, according to the manufacturer, Vir Biotechnology.^{1}

This investigational therapy is a prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)–targeted, PRO-XTEN dual-masked T-cell engager intended for the treatment of metastatic prostate cancer. By utilizing a “masked” delivery system, the therapy remains inactive in the bloodstream and only becomes potent upon reaching the tumor microenvironment, a mechanism intended to increase the therapeutic window and reduce systemic adverse events.

The ongoing phase 1 trial is designed to measure the safety and efficacy of VIR-5500 monotherapy in late-line metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). Additionally, the trial evaluates VIR-5500 in combination with an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor for patients in early-line mCRPC and metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer.

The monotherapy expansion cohort in late-line mCRPC is the first to begin enrollment following monotherapy dose-escalation data that showed a favorable safety profile and promising anti-tumor activity.

These data, presented at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology Genitourinary Cancers Symposium (ASCO GU),^{2} led to the selection of an 800/2000/3500 µg/kg step-up dosing regimen administered once every 3 weeks.

This cohort will monitor safety and efficacy through prostate-specific antigen response rates and objective response rates (ORR) in patients who are refractory after multiple prior therapies. Dose-escalation of VIR-5500 in combination with enzalutamide (Xtandi) also continues in early-line mCRPC patients, with first patient dosing in combination dose-expansion cohorts expected over the coming months.

“I think we’re heading toward immunotherapy that works impressively for metastatic prostate cancer with proof of concept that we can abrogate the CRS [cytokine release syndrome],” lead author Johann S. De Bono, MD, said during a presentation of the data at ASCO GU. Johann de Bono, MD, is Regius Professor of Cancer Research and a professor in experimental cancer medicine at The Institute of Cancer Research and The Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust. “This agent was well tolerated with minimal CRS despite not giving prophylactic steroids.”

“The initiation of the VIR-5500 expansion cohorts underscores the significant momentum behind this program and the enthusiasm we are seeing across the clinical community,” Marianne De Backer, PhD, MBA, MSc, said in a news release. De Backer is chief executive officer of Vir Biotechnology. “We are encouraged by the promising antitumor activity shown in the phase 1 data announced earlier this year and look forward to collaborating with Astellas after closing of the transaction to explore VIR-5500’s potential to make a meaningful difference across the spectrum of metastatic prostate cancer.”

## Background About Phase 1 Trial

The objectives of the study were to characterize safety, pharmacokinetics profiles, and antitumor activity. Fifty-one heavily pretreated patients with mCRPC received 1 or more doses of VIR-5500. No dose-limiting toxicities were reported. The incidence of related grade 3 or higher adverse events was low and CRS was limited to grade 1 and 2. Investigators reported an ORR of 67% in 4 out of 6 RECIST-evaluable patients.

## About VIR-5500

T-cell engagers are potent antitumor therapies that harness the immune system to target and eliminate cancer cells. VIR-5500 is an investigational PRO-XTEN dual-masked T-cell engager under evaluation in an open-label, nonrandomized phase 1 trial, and is the only PSMA-directed agent of its kind currently in clinical development.

This dual-masking approach is designed to limit activity to the tumor microenvironment, potentially reducing the toxicity seen with unmasked engagers while improving efficacy and tolerability. Additionally, the masking strategy may prolong circulation time in an inactive state, supporting the possibility of less frequent dosing.

The PRIMARY2 phase 3 trial found that PSMA PET-CT in men with normal or equivocal MRI results safely halved the number of prostate biopsies, maintained non-inferior detection of clinically significant cancer, and reduced insignificant cancer diagnosis by more than half.

Adding prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET-CT to the diagnostic pathway for men with normal or equivocal MRI findings safely halved the number of prostate biopsies performed while maintaining equivalent detection of clinically significant prostate cancer, according to results from PRIMARY2 (NCT05154162), a multicenter, phase 3 randomized controlled trial presented at the 41st Annual Congress of the European Association of Urology in London, United Kingdom.^{1}

The trial met both co-primary end points. Murphy noted that the findings build on the original PRIMARY trial, which established PSMA PET-CT as a tool with improved negative predictive value for sPCa compared to MRI alone, and argued that the results now support a formal shift in practice.

# U.K. clinical trial validates PET-CT surveillance for patients with advanced head/neck cancer

April 27, 2016 · Staff News Brief

PET-CT-guided surveillance to assess the response of patients with squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck and advanced nodal disease following chemoradiotherapy is used at some cancer treatment centers to reduce unnecessary neck dissection. Its efficacy with respect to patient outcomes has now been validated by the results of a randomized prospective clinical trial conducted at 37 cancer treatment centers throughout the United Kingdom.

Approximately 80% of the patients assigned to the PET-CT surveillance arm of the study were able to avoid neck dissection, according to study findings published online March 23 in the New England Journal of Medicine. Non-invasive PET-CT surveillance was more cost effective, and improved patient safety, comfort, and convenience.

Head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCC) are the most common type of head and neck cancers. Because a large percentage of patients do not have a complete response to chemotherapy and radiotherapy treatment, subsequent neck dissection is frequently performed. This procedure is an up-to-three hour long surgery associated with a high level of complications and morbidity, and hospitalization of up to a week in duration.

The ability of PET/CT to identify structural and metabolic abnormalities provides image-guidance for surgeons and identifies patients who have had a complete response to treatment. But because outcomes had not been formally validated in 2007, the University of Birmingham Institute of Head and Neck Studies and the University of Warwick Clinical Trials Unit initiated one.

Image: U.K. clinical trial validates PET-CT surveillance for patients with advanced head/neck cancer

The clinical trial enrolled 564 patients from October 2007 to September 2012. Seventy nine percent of the patients had N2a or N2b nodal disease. They were assigned to either a planned surgery arm or a PET-CT surveillance exam performed 12 weeks after completion of chemoradiotherapy. Both groups were matched and equivalent with respect to age, sex, tumor sites, tumor and nodal stages, and HPV status. All patients were followed for up to five years.

Lead author and chief investigator Professor Hisham Mehanna, PhD., director of the Institute of Head and Neck Studies at the University of Birmingham, and colleagues reported that only 54 of the 282 patients in the PET-CT group required neck dissections, or 19.1%, whereas 221 surgeries were performed in the planned surgery group, or 78.4%. The number of complications following surgery was also lower: 22 in the surveillance group compared to 83 in the planned surgery group. Survival rates for the two groups were comparable.

The authors recommend that patients with strong FDG uptake should have a neck dissection. As for patients with equivocal FDG uptake, the authors wrote, “We recommend that patients with an equivocal FDG uptake should continue to undergo neck dissection, especially if they have HPV-negative disease. However, patients with HPV-positive cancers who have enlarged nodes but no FDG uptake after chemoradiotherapy may be considered for close follow-up with serial CT or PET-CT; this strategy may spare even more patients from undergoing a neck dissection.”

“This study provides level 1evidence to support image-guided surveillance as the standard of care for advanced nodal disease in patients treated with primary chemoradiotherapy,” said Dr. Mehanna.

Your participation will directly advance the understanding of CTVT transmission in the UK while helping establish faster, more reliable diagnostic pathways for veterinary practices nationwide.

Postdoctoral Scientist

### Background & Clinical Relevance

Canine transmissible venereal tumour is a unique infectious cancer transmitted via living cells during direct contact, such as mating, sniffing, or licking. Once diagnosed, CTVT is highly treatable with vincristine chemotherapy.

While CTVT was historically eradicated from the UK, incidence is currently rising due to the increased importation of dogs from endemic regions, particularly Eastern Europe. A recent case report confirmed active CTVT transmission within the UK for the first time in over 50 years.

Because UK prevalence has remained low for decades, many practitioners are unfamiliar with CTVT's presentation - especially atypical extragenital cases. Standard diagnostic methods (cytology, histology, and travel history) are not always conclusive. The LINE-MYC PCR assay provides the clarity needed for accurate diagnosis and prompt treatment.

## Recrutement pour un essai clinique multicentrique pour le traitement par cimentation des ostéosarcomes appendiculaires chez le chien.

Les cliniciens du Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Vétérinaire d’Oniris et la société TheraVet ® réalisent actuellement une étude clinique prospective multicentrique sur le traitement de l’ostéosarcome du chien avec un ciment osseux injectable (BIOCERA-VET®).

### Qu’est-ce que l’ostéosarcome ?

#### Descriptif de la maladie

L’ostéosarcome est le cancer des os le plus fréquent chez le chien, représentant 85% de tous les cancers osseux canins. Ce cancer, très agressif, est à l’origine de fractures pathologiques et de douleur aigüe. La durée de survie moyenne de l’animal sans traitement se situe entre 4 et 5 mois et moins de 10% des chiens atteints d’ostéosarcome survivent 1 an.

L’ostéosarcome est actuellement traité par amputation ou par des chirurgies conservatrices des membres associées à de la chimiothérapie, qui permettent d’augmenter la survie à 1 an jusqu’à 50 %(2). Toutefois, 50% des chiens survivant 1 an et plus grâce à ces traitements sont susceptibles de développer des métastases, avec une espérance de survie médiane ne dépassant pas 9 mois(3). Dans certain cas, l’amputation n’est pas la meilleure option, en particulier pour les chiens de grande ou très grande race, surtout s’ils souffrent de troubles neurologiques ou orthopédiques concomitants (dysplasie, maladie dégénérative articulaire...).

En outre, les propriétaires de ces animaux recherchent de plus en plus souvent des traitements palliatifs afin d’éviter l’amputation. Enfin, les chirurgies conservatrices ayant recours à des endoprothèses et des allogreffes d’os cortical sont des procédures complexes, non applicables à tous les sites affectés et qui peuvent entrainer des complicatios majeures. Il existe donc un véritable besoin de nouvelles techniques alternatives. 

Au cours des dernières années, le Professeur Olivier Gauthier, Professeur de chirurgie des petits animaux et dentisterie vétérinaire, a mis au point une technique de chirurgie conservatrice mini-invasive consistant en l’injection de ciment phosphocalcique au niveau du site tumoral. Les résultats de ces travaux précurseurs ont ainsi montré qu’une telle technique permet de conserver la fonction du membre et de soulager immédiatement et durablement la douleur, améliorant ainsi considérablement le bien-être de l’animal.  

### L'étude clinique menée à Oniris

#### Découvrir l'étude

  * La phase de recrutement est actuellement ouverte à Oniris. Elle consiste à inclure des chiens atteints d’ostéosarcome appendiculaire.
  * Une dizaine de chien ont déjà été traités avec succès par cette méthode.
  * L’injection du ciment phosphocalcique à l’intérieur de l’os rongé par la tumeur. se fait par voie percutanée sous anesthésie générale et sous contrôle radioscopique. Elle ne nécessite pas d’intervention massive. Une incision de la peau sur deux centimètres suffit, à introduire la canule dans l’os.

In der vorliegenden Studie untersuchen wir die Sicherheit und Verträglichkeit der oralen Verabreichung von Vinorelbin bei Hunden mit Tumorerkrankungen. Ziel dieser frühen klinischen Phase-I-Studie ist es, eine geeignete Dosis zu bestimmen, die gut verträglich ist und keine schwerwiegenden Nebenwirkungen verursacht.

## Informationen zur Studie

Was ist Vinorelbin?

Vinorelbin ist ein Medikament gegen Krebs bei Menschen und Hunden. Studien zufolge können insbesondere Hunde mit Lymphom, histiozytärem Sarkom, Mastozytom und Lungenkarzinom von diesem Medikament profitieren. In der Tiermedizin steht es bislang jedoch nur intravenös zur Verfügung. Das kann bei einigen Tieren zu erhöhtem Stress, Angst oder Aggressivität führen und die Behandlung zusätzlich erschweren.

### Einschlusskriterien

  * Hunde mit einer Tumorerkrankung, bei denen eine Standardtherapie nicht mehr infrage kommt (z.B. grosse inoperable Tumore oder metastasierte Tumore) oder nicht durchgeführt werden kann (z.B. Kosten)
  * Hunde mit gutem Allgemeinzustand
  *  Körpergewicht > 5 kg

### Vorteile

Ihr Tier erhält eine einfache Therapieoption, die möglicherweise wirksam ist. Gleichzeitig helfen Sie dabei, eine neue Therapieform für zukünftige Patienten zu etablieren.

Ein Teil der Kosten wird durch eine Stiftung übernommen.

## Hintergrundinformationen

In der Humanmedizin ist die orale Gabe von Vinorelbin längst etabliert, da sie für die Patientinnen und Patienten deutlich bequemer ist. Ältere Patienten profitieren davon besonders.

Auch bei Hunden könnte eine orale Chemotherapie den Klinikbesuch vereinfachen und stressfreier gestalten – sowohl für das Tier als auch für den Halter.

## Was ist das Ziel?

Mit unserer Studie wollen wir eine sichere orale Dosis von Vinorelbin bei Hunden mit Tumoren bestimmen. Das soll helfen, eine Grundlage für zukünftige orale Behandlungskonzepte zu schaffen.

## Was passiert bei der Studie?

Die Behandlung besteht aus einer einzigen Dosis Vinorelbin zum Einnehmen. Vorher sind nötige Tests durchzuführen, wie Blut- und Urinuntersuchungen, Röntgen des Brustkorbs und Ultraschall des Bauchraums. Um die Tiere nicht unnötig zu belasten, werden bestimmte frühere Analysen akzeptiert, sofern sie nicht veraltet sind.

Nach sieben Tagen erfolgt eine Nachkontrolle in Form einer klinischen Untersuchung und einer Blutuntersuchung.

>  Wilt u bijdragen aan baanbrekend kankeronderzoek voor katten en mensen? Help kankerbehandeling vooruit!

Doel van deze studie
Triple-negatieve borstkanker (TNBC) bij vrouwen is een agressief type kanker met weinig behandelopties. Evenals mensen kunnen van nature kwaadaardige borsttumoren ontwikkelen (mammaire adenocarcinomen) die erg vergelijkbaar zijn met agressieve borstkanker bij mensen.

Dit project test een nieuwe therapie die zich richt op een specifieke pathway in kankercellen, met als doel het risico dat de kanker terugkomt of zich verspreidt te verkleinen. Katten die aan de studie deelnemen, ontvangen deze therapie naast routine chirurgie en helpen zo om de behandeling van kanker bij zowel katten als mensen te verbeteren.

# Científicos de la UNAM prueban nanopartículas de plata para frenar el cáncer en perros y gatos

## Una formulación desarrollada por la UNAM y dos universidades públicas se prueba en ocho perros y gatos; los primeros resultados reportan mejoría clínica y detención de la progresión de tumores

Por: Laura Toribio

03 de noviembre de 2026 - 20:41 Hrs

Image: Uno de los casos es Ody, perrita de 14 años con osteosarcoma y metástasis pulmonar; su pronóstico de vida era de entre uno y dos meses.Uno de los casos es Ody, perrita de 14 años con osteosarcoma y metástasis pulmonar; su pronóstico de vida era de entre uno y dos meses.Especial

Atacar el cáncer sin castigar al resto del organismo es el desafío detrás de una investigación mexicana que lleva la nanotecnología a la oncología veterinaria. Científicos de la UNAM y de dos universidades públicas prueban una formulación de nanopartículas de plata en perros y gatos con tumores, con resultados preliminares que apuntan a frenar la progresión de la enfermedad y mejorar la calidad de vida de los pacientes.

El desarrollo se llama Argovit y es resultado del trabajo del Centro de Nanociencias y Nanotecnología (CNyN) de la UNAM, en colaboración con las universidades autónomas de Baja California y de Guadalajara. Su objetivo es aprovechar las propiedades de la plata a escala nanométrica para combatir las neoplasias mediante una formulación que, según sus desarrolladores, busca actuar selectivamente sobre las células tumorales.

Ocho animales, entre perros y gatos, participan actualmente en el protocolo experimental. Aunque todos han presentado avances, el equipo todavía busca determinar en qué tipos de cáncer funciona mejor, qué dosis son adecuadas y en qué etapas de la enfermedad puede ofrecer mayores beneficios.

Los resultados todavía no permiten hablar de una cura, pero uno de los casos que muestra el potencial de la investigación es el de Ody, una perrita de 14 años con cáncer en un hueso y metástasis pulmonar.

Cuando comenzó el tratamiento, en abril de 2026, tenía poca movilidad y los veterinarios estimaban que le quedaban uno o dos meses de vida. Cuatro meses después, los estudios mostraron que la metástasis persistía, pero la enfermedad había dejado de avanzar. También recuperó movilidad y volvió a salir de paseo.

“No estamos eliminando el cáncer, lo que sí es que mejoró la calidad de vida y la progresión de la enfermedad a un punto metastásico”, explicó Norma Elvira Díaz Ramos, médica veterinaria que participa en el protocolo.

La apuesta científica está en las propiedades de las nanopartículas. Nina Bogdanchikova, investigadora del CNyN y responsable de la Red Internacional de Bionanotecnología con Impacto en Biomedicina, Alimentación y Bioseguridad, explicó que las partículas de plata pueden tener aplicaciones médicas, pero su utilización enfrenta un obstáculo: la toxicidad de algunas formulaciones.

Argovit busca resolver ese problema con una composición que, de acuerdo con la investigadora, no presenta toxicidad ni efectos secundarios y puede ser hasta 200 veces más efectiva contra las neoplasias.

La primera etapa del proyecto se concentra en evaluar la respuesta de los animales mediante radiografías, análisis de sangre y seguimiento clínico. El propósito es ampliar la muestra y establecer las condiciones en las que la formulación podría utilizarse con mayor eficacia.

El horizonte de la investigación va más allá de la medicina veterinaria: sus responsables contemplan que, una vez concluidos los estudios en animales, pueda explorarse su aplicación en humanos. Para llegar a ese punto todavía hacen falta tiempo, recursos y nuevas etapas de investigación.

Por ahora, el desafío es demostrar científicamente que las nanopartículas de plata pueden convertirse en una herramienta contra el cáncer.

# ReachGlio: nuevo ensayo clínico para perros con glioma de alto grado

17 septiembre, 2026 Hospital Veterinario Puchol Neurologia

El Hospital Veterinario Puchol ha iniciado el reclutamiento de pacientes para ReachGlio, un Ensayo Clínico Veterinario dirigido a perros con diagnóstico presuntivo de glioma de alto grado, uno de los tumores cerebrales más complejos en neurología y oncología veterinaria.

El estudio ha sido autorizado por laAgencia Española de Medicamentos y Productos Sanitarios (AEMPS)y está financiado en el marco de la convocatoria europea TRANSCAN-3, orientada a impulsar la investigación traslacional en cáncer.

El Ensayo Clínico Veterinario se desarrollará en elHospital Veterinario Puchol, en el marco de un proyecto de investigación promovido por la Unidad de Neurooncología del Instituto de Salud Carlos III, y coordinado por la Universidad Camilo José Cela.

Más allá de evaluar una nueva estrategia terapéutica en el contexto de un ensayo clínico, ReachGlio busca responder a una pregunta especialmente relevante en neurooncología:
Esta información es imprescindible para comprender mejor la enfermedad y, particularmente, para interpretar los resultados obtenidos durante el ensayo.

## El Hospital Veterinario Puchol desarrollará la fase clínica veterinaria

La incorporación del Hospital Veterinario Puchol al proyecto permitirá trasladar esta investigación al contexto clínico, trabajando con pacientes caninos con tumores que aparecen de forma espontánea, dentro de un entorno clínico especializado y bajo un protocolo específicamente autorizado.

El hospital será el centro encargado de desarrollar el ensayo clínico, con participación de su Servicio de Neurología y de los recursos necesarios para la evaluación clínica, el diagnóstico por imagen, la administración del tratamiento y el seguimiento de los pacientes.

Los procedimientos específicamente contemplados dentro del protocolo de investigación, incluyendo el tratamiento, las resonancias de seguimiento y las analíticas vinculadas al estudio, están financiados en el marco de TRANSCAN-3 y no supondrán un coste adicional para los propietarios.

Sin embargo, el principal valor de este proyecto no es económico.

ReachGlio representa la posibilidad de que determinados pacientes con una enfermedad neurológica grave accedan a una estrategia terapéutica experimental única dentro de un Ensayo Clínico regulado, protocolizado y estrechamente monitorizado, pudiéndose beneficiar de las nuevas oportunidades terapéuticas que ofrecen moléculas actualmente en desarrollo

Y representa también algo esencial para el futuro de la medicina veterinaria: seguir generando evidencia allí donde todavía existen preguntas sin respuesta.

### Información para veterinarios

El reclutamiento de pacientes comenzó el 1 de septiembre de 2026.

Los veterinarios que atiendan a un perro con una lesión intracraneal compatible con un glioma de alto grado pueden contactar con el Hospital Veterinario Puchol para valorar conjuntamente si el paciente cumple inicialmente los criterios necesarios para ser considerado candidato al ensayo.

La puesta en marcha de ReachGlio supone un nuevo paso en el compromiso del Hospital Veterinario Puchol con una medicina basada en la especialización, el rigor científico, la innovación y la investigación clínica, especialmente en enfermedades complejas en las que todavía es necesario seguir avanzando.

# 64Cu-SAR-bisPSMA Earns FDA Breakthrough Designation in Recurrent Prostate Cancer

Author(s)Cancer Network Staff

Fact checked by: Roman Fabbricatore, Nicole Canfora Lupo

The FDA granted breakthrough therapy designation to 64Cu-SAR-bisPSMA for PSMA PET imaging in men with suspected biochemical recurrence of prostate cancer.

The FDA has granted breakthrough therapy designation to copper Cu 64 (64Cu)-SAR-bisPSMA for PET imaging of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)–positive lesions in men with prostate cancer who have suspected recurrence based on elevated serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, according to a news release from the developer, Clarity Pharmaceuticals.^{1} According to the company, this is the first breakthrough therapy designation granted to a PSMA PET imaging agent.

The designation was supported by data from the phase 2 Co-PSMA trial (NCT06907641), the phase 1/2a COBRA trial (NCT05249127), and real-world evidence. Topline data from the phase 3 AMPLIFY (NCT06970847) and CLARIFY (NCT06056830) trials are expected in the first half of 2027 and are intended to support an FDA application for 64Cu-SAR-bisPSMA.

## What data supported the breakthrough designation for 64Cu-SAR-bisPSMA?

The investigator-initiated Co-PSMA trial compared 64Cu-SAR-bisPSMA with standard gallium Ga 68 (68Ga)–PSMA-11 PET/CT in 50 patients with biochemical recurrence (BCR) following radical prostatectomy, with a median PSA of 0.43 ng/mL.^{1} The trial met its primary end point, with a mean of 1.26 lesions detected per patient with next-day (24-hour) 64Cu-SAR-bisPSMA imaging vs 0.48 lesions with 68Ga-PSMA-11 (P <.0001). Patient-level positivity was 78% (n = 39/50) vs 36% (n = 18/50), respectively, and reader agreement was higher with 64Cu-SAR-bisPSMA (Cohen κ, 0.94 vs 0.75). Planned management changed in 44% of patients after 64Cu-SAR-bisPSMA imaging. Findings were published in European Urology.^{2}

CLARIFY is a single-arm, open-label diagnostic trial with blinded review evaluating 64Cu-SAR-bisPSMA in patients with untreated, histopathology-confirmed high-risk prostate cancer before radical prostatectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection. Target enrollment was reached in October 2026.

Both trials have completed recruitment and are in follow-up, according to Clarity. The company plans to use the results to support an FDA application for 64Cu-SAR-bisPSMA as a diagnostic imaging agent in both the BCR and pre–definitive therapy settings.

  2. Khan S, Papa N, Kneebone A, et al. Prospective comparison of 64Copper [64Cu]SAR-bisPSMA vs 68Gallium [68Ga] PSMA-11 PET/CT for biochemical recurrence of prostate cancer following radical prostatectomy (Co-PSMA Trial). Eur Urol. 2026;89(6):512-520. doi:10.1016/j.eururo.2026.03.001

# SNMMI: PSMA-PET/CT-guided biopsy improves prostate cancer detection

Will Morton

Oct 7, 2026

The Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging (SNMMI) has highlighted a study showing that biopsies guided by prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET/CT detect more prostate cancer than standard systematic biopsies in men with negative MRI scans. 

To determining whether PSMA-PET can refine risk stratification and guide targeted sampling for these men, Farolfi and colleagues recruited 63 men with negative or inconclusive MRI scans. Participants underwent gallium-68 PSMA-11 PET/CT followed by PET fusion-guided prostate biopsy. The researchers assessed the diagnostic performance of PSMA-PET/CT–guided targeted biopsy versus systematic biopsy.

Image: PET-CT scan images showing axial and coronal views of abdomen with arrows indicating focal lesions in kidney and lower abdomen regionsUpstage with PET-guided biopsy. A 70-y-old patient with suspicious prostate cancer (PI-RADS 2; initial PSA, 15.9; PSA density, 0.4). Further, combining PSMA-PET/CT-targeted biopsy with systematic biopsy increased the clinically significant prostate cancer detection rate to 41%.

# PSMA PET/CT Scan Reduces Need for Prostate Cancer Biopsies by 50%

March 18, 2026 By The ASCO Post Staff 3 min read

Share

A PSMA-11 PET/CT scan with gallium Ga-68 led to the identification of more aggressive prostate cancer cells in men with equivocal or nonsuspicious findings on multiparametric MRI than a standard biopsy, according to first results from the phase III PRIMARY2 trial presented at the 2026 Annual Congress of the European Association of Urology (Abstract GC26-006). 

The PSMA PET/CT scan resulted in half as many men requiring a biopsy than standard processes and reduced the diagnosis of insignificant prostate cancers without missing any clinically significant cancers. 

“Getting told you have a risk of prostate cancer is a huge cause of anxiety and concern. Our findings show that PSMA PET/CT after MRI offers a 'belt and braces' approach that can determine which people have a clinically significant cancer, and which people are at low risk and don’t need a biopsy or further testing," said co-lead study author Louise Emmett, BSc(Hons), MBChB, FRACP, FAANMS, MD, Director of Theranostics and Nuclear Medicine at St Vincent's Hospital, Sydney. "PRIMARY2 is the largest of a series of studies undertaken by this group, exploring whether PSMA PET/CT scanning could improve prostate cancer diagnosis and reduce unnecessary biopsies for patients.”

The investigator-initiated, multicenter, randomized, controlled phase III PRIMARY2 trial enrolled 660 men from across seven Australian hospitals who had a prostate-specific antigen level below 20 ng/mL and PI-RADS 2 with high clinical risk or PI-RADS 3 who had not yet undergone a biopsy. Patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to either pelvic-only Ga-68-PSMA-11 PET/CT scan or systemic transperineal prostate biopsy. In the investigational arm, if results of the PSMA PET/CT scan were positive, patients underwent a targeted biopsy, and if results were negative patients could avoid a biopsy. 

“PSMA PET/CT scanning makes prostate cancer cells light up in a remarkable way, particularly in more aggressive cancers. It’s rare to see such strong imaging that could be so powerful in the clinic. Incorporating this testing into clinical care could help to address the major challenge of prostate cancer overdiagnosis, which leads to at best unnecessary and at worst harmful treatment for cancers that would never cause any harm,” said presenting author James Buteau, MD, FRACP, FRCPC, Nuclear Medicine Physician at Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre.

The coprimary endpoints were the proportion of patients with clinically significant prostate cancer and proportion of patients in the PSMA PET/CT arm who could avoid biopsy. A key secondary endpoint was the proportion of patients with clinically insignificant prostate cancer. 

Key Findings 

In the PSMA PET/CT arm, 49% of patients were able to avoid biopsy (95% confidence interval [CI] = 44%–55%; P < .0001). 

In the control arm, 16% of patients had significant prostate cancer, which was considered a Gleason score of seven or higher, compared with 12% in the investigational arm, for a difference of –3.7% (95% CI = –8.0% to 1.5%; P = .0093). The proportion of patients with a Gleason score of 4 + 3 or higher was 4.8% in the control arm and 4.2% in the investigational arm. The rate of insignificant prostate cancer was 32% in the biopsy arm and 14% in the PSMA PET/CT arm, for a difference of –18% (97.5% CI = –25% to –11%; P < .0001). 

“This well-conducted trial shows that incorporating PSMA PET/CT in men with low or intermediate risk lesions—defined by MRI as PI-RADS 2 or 3—significantly reduced the number of unnecessary biopsies and the diagnosis of clinically insignificant prostate cancer. Importantly, this didn’t compromise the detection of clinically significant disease," stated Derya Tilki, MD, Member of the EAU Scientific Congress Office and a Senior Consultant Urologist at Martini-Klinik Prostate Cancer Center, Germany. "These results support consideration of PSMA PET/CT in the diagnostic work-up of appropriately selected patients. I congratulate the investigators on their study.”

The project will test the effectiveness of immunomodulatory drug Enzistat in treating solid tumours caused by naturally occurring cancers, including soft tissue sarcoma, mast cell tumour and melanoma.

Professor Rachel Allavena from UQ’s School of Veterinary Science said owners who had been told their dog’s cancer was terminal or their pet’s tumours were inoperable should apply for the trial.

“The 6-week treatment consists of oral tablet Enzistat being administered twice daily, regular consultations, blood samples and biopsies,” Professor Allavena said.

“Enzistat is designed to target advanced cancers by activating the patient’s immune system.

“Enzistat is designed to be an oral, off-the-shelf drug that provides high-end immunotherapy results without the complexity of hospital-based infusions.”

### プレスリリースを公開しました

公益財団法人日本小動物医療センター、国立大学法人山口大学共同獣医学部、かもがわ動物医療センターは、日本全薬工業株式会社と連携し、犬の口腔内悪性黒色腫（メラノーマ）に対する「抗イヌPD-1抗体」の企業治験を開始しました。

プレスリリース全文（PDF）を見る

### 治験の概要

#### 対象となる病気

犬の口腔内に発生する悪性黒色腫（メラノーマ）は、悪性度が高く、周囲の組織への浸潤や肺などへの転移を起こしやすい腫瘍です。手術や放射線治療が主な治療法ですが、進行した例や再発した例では治療の選択肢が限られています。

#### 治験薬について

人の医療では、抗PD-1抗体はがんに対する免疫の「ブレーキ」を解除し、患者さん自身の免疫で腫瘍を攻撃することを目指す治療として使われています。ただし、人の治療薬を犬にそのまま使うことはできません。この治験で使用するのは、犬に使うことを前提に開発された「抗イヌPD-1抗体」です。

抗イヌPD-1抗体は、現時点では動物用医薬品として承認されていない開発中の薬剤です。この治験は、定められた治験実施計画書に基づいて、有効性と安全性を評価するために行われます。治験で得られたデータは、将来の製造販売承認申請の資料として使われる予定です。

### 治験への参加について

口腔内悪性黒色腫（メラノーマ）と診断された犬のうち、定められた条件を満たす犬が対象です。「うちの子が対象になるか知りたい」という段階でもご相談いただけます。ただし、参加には条件があり、すべての犬が参加できるわけではありません。

参加にあたってご理解いただきたいこと

  * 全身状態や腫瘍の進行具合によっては、参加できない場合があります。
  * 細胞診・病理組織検査など、参加前に必要な検査があります。
  * 2週間に1回、計6回の来院が必要です。
  * 治験期間中は、使用できる薬剤に制限があります。
  * 治験に参加しても、治療効果が得られることを保証するものではありません。予想される副作用などの不利益や費用負担については、個別にご説明します。

# Are Pet Owners Really at Greater Risk of Cancer?

## The surprising results of a new "big data" study of cancer rates in pet owners.

Posted September 1, 2016

Image: Jean-Paul CHASSENET/123RF

Source: Jean-Paul CHASSENET/123RF

Our pets might give us unconditional love, but they can also give us a host of things we really don’t want. These include Lyme disease, leptospirosis, giardia, ring worms and salmonella. Indeed, some researchers have even claimed that we might get cancer from our pets. Thus pet lovers will find a new study by researchers from the University of Arizona reassuring. Using a data set of over 120,000 women, they found there was no relationship between owning pets and developing nine types of cancer. The research team was led by David Garcia of the University of Arizona. They used a huge existing medical data set to investigate the relationship between pet ownership and the risk of nine forms of cancer (breast, colorectal, endometrial, kidney, bladder, stomach, lung, ovary, and lymphoma). Their findings generally put to rest any concerns you might have that pets cause cancer. But their research also reveals some unexpected non-cancer related health differences between pet owners and non-owners.

Pet owners will be glad to know that Garcia’s team found no evidence that pet ownership was associated with overall rates of cancer in women. Nor was pet-owning significantly linked with any of the nine specific types of cancers. After adjusting for age, the researchers did find that the cat owners were 15% more likely to have developed lung cancer, but cat owners were also 29% less likely to have contracted endometrial cancer.

Author(s)Abi Bautista-Alejandre, Assistant Editor

The latest updates relating to animal care establishments and platforms.

In Sacramento, California, the University of California, Davis (UC Davis) has launched the Translational Brain Tumor Center, a new research initiative connecting its veterinary and human medicine programs to advance brain cancer treatments across species. Meanwhile, in Logan, Utah, Purina Pro Plan Veterinary has opened a student wellness center at Utah State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine, the latest initiative under its Pro Plan Veterinary Support Mission. And in Dallas, Texas, CityVet has opened CityVet Bishop Arts under a local veterinarian.

## UC Davis opens center focused on brain tumors in people and pets

The UC Davis Translational Brain Tumor Center connects researchers and clinicians from the UC Davis Weill School of Veterinary Medicine and UC Davis Health to study brain cancers across species. The center launches with two active National Cancer Institute–funded clinical trials recruiting dogs diagnosed with or suspected of having glioma: the CARE trial and the PRISM trial. The CARE trial is evaluating an experimental drug intended to make glioma cells more vulnerable to radiation therapy, while the PRISM trial tracks tumor progression and combines clinical data with genetic and immune profiling to identify subtypes that may support more personalized treatment.

Companion dogs can develop brain tumors that share characteristics with human cancers—including genetic changes, neurological symptoms, patterns of growth, and treatment resistance—making them a relevant population for studying naturally occurring disease under clinical conditions.

The center supports advanced imaging, molecular research, biobanking, multidisciplinary clinical care, and education in comparative neuro-oncology.

## Purina Pro Plan announces veterinary student wellness center at Utah State University in Logan, Utah

Purina Pro Plan Veterinary has opened the Purina Pro Plan Wellness Center at Utah State University’s (USU) College of Veterinary Medicine, providing students with dedicated space for one-on-one sessions with wellness specialists and areas for meditation and mindfulness practice. The opening comes as USU continues to build its 4-year Doctor of Veterinary Medicine program, which welcomed its inaugural class of 39 students in August 2025 and its second class of 77 students this fall.

“The Purina Pro Plan Wellness Center represents our commitment to making wellbeing an integral part of veterinary education,” said Michael Bishop, director of student affairs for USU’s College of Veterinary Medicine, in a news release.^{2}

Article metrics

Traditionally regarded as conduits for afferent information, selected sensory axons can also act as peripheral effector units by releasing neurotransmitters and neuropeptides from their peripheral terminals. These local actions can regulate vascular tone, vascular permeability, immune-cell activity, inflammation, tissue repair, and, in specific organs, contractile function. This mini-review builds on the presentation “The Motor Function of the Sensory Axon,” delivered at the International Veterinary Emergency and Critical Care Society, held in San Diego, California, on September 4th, 2025. As part of a collection documenting scientific contributions from the meeting, it preserves and shares the key concepts presented on the peripheral effector functions of sensory axons. This review explores the efferent-like functions of sensory axons in biological processes, including neurogenic inflammation, peripheral immune modulation, and vascular control, in the context of animal physiology and disease. These actions are distinguished from the conventional sensory contribution to reflexes and motor control, which requires central synaptic processing and motor-neuron output.

### 1.2 Clinical implications and disease relevance

The clinical implications of the efferent-like functions of sensory axons in veterinary medicine are far-reaching, particularly in chronic pain syndromes, inflammatory disorders, and tissue repair. Recognizing the efferent role of sensory neurons enables veterinarians to approach certain conditions not only as immune-driven or mechanical issues but as neurogenic pathologies with a strong neuroimmune interface.

Although distinct from the peripheral effector functions that form the principal focus of this review, the recruitment of sensory afferents also has important clinical applications in veterinary neurorehabilitation. Sensory afferents provide conventional input to spinal interneurons, central pattern-generating networks and motor neurons, thereby influencing reflex excitability and locomotor output. Incorporating this knowledge into veterinary diagnostics and therapeutics has the potential to transform how conditions such as chronic pain, dermatitis, arthritis, and impaired wound healing are treated. Therapies targeting the efferent functions of sensory axons, through neuropeptide modulation, receptor blockade, or gene therapy, may offer more effective, targeted, and lasting relief for animals.

The Cornell University Hospital for Animals is actively engaged in clinical studies that work towards applicable treatments and cures for our patients. Please consider informing owners of eligible patients about relevant studies, and help us move the research forward!

#### Featured Trial:  Pain treatment for canine cancer patients

  * BACKGROUND: Some dogs with cancer, especially end-stage cancer patients or patients with dermatitis secondary to radiation therapy, experience pain that cannot be adequately controlled with oral medications given by their owners at home. Depending on the site of pain, an epidural injection can provide pain relief superior to oral medications, sometimes with fewer side effects. The duration of pain relief is variable but may last several weeks. Repeating the injection requires heavy sedation or general anesthesia each time, and this puts the dog at risk for anesthetic complications, is time consuming, and can be prohibitively expensive.
  * METHODS: The Anesthesiology and Pain Medicine Service at the Cornell University Hospital for Animals (CUHA) is currently investigating a prototype device that consists of an epidural catheter placed under fluoroscopic guidance and connected to an access port that is implanted under the skin over a dog’s back under brief general anesthesia. # Controlled Clinical Trials in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Winning Value Proposition

Author(s)Donald de Korte, Alan Boyce, and Karin Kanewske Turner

Listen

0:00 / 0:00

[Input]

### Key Takeaways

  * Clinical trials often face recruitment challenges, with Africa underrepresented despite its potential for research in non-communicable diseases.
  * Africa's genetic diversity is crucial for oncology and precision medicine research, offering unique insights into treatment efficacy.
  * Declining donor funding has left untapped research capacity in Africa, with trained professionals and infrastructure available for clinical trials.
  * Challenges include limited electronic health records, slow regulatory approvals, and ethical requirements for post-trial medication provision.
  * Addressing these challenges could accelerate trials, provide economic benefits, and improve healthcare access in Africa.
SHOW MORE

Persistent recruitment delays, high dropout rates, and missed timelines continue to slow global clinical trials, while data show that sub-Saharan Africa offers a largely untapped opportunity with established research capacity, large patient pools, and strong enrollment and retention performance.

### 

## Key numbers at a glance

  * <56% of clinical trials reach their target enrollment.

  * 43% pooled dropout rate reported across chronic disease trials.

  * ~20% of trials finish on time, with a 12.2-month median delay.

  * 1.1% of global clinical trials are conducted in Africa.

  * African site networks report >80% consent and 85%–96% retention, highlighting strong recruitment and participant engagement.

The conduct of controlled clinical trials in traditional settings is faced with many challenges often resulting in important delays in the execution of studies. In most geographic settings, there is a limited pool of eligible patients because of small catchment areas and competition for participation in other studies. Many studies are faced with slow recruitment because eligibility criteria have increased and trials become more complex. In a metanalysis of clinical trials in the UK less than 56% of clinical trials reached the target sample size.^{1 }Another metanalysis of clinical trials in chronic disease found a pooled dropout rate of 43%.^{2} And lastly, a metanalysis of 2,542 randomized clinical trials showed that around one out of five studies completes within the planned timeframe, and that the median delay in completion is 12.2 months.^{3}

## Africa remains underrepresented in global clinical research

According to estimates, only 1.1% of clinical trials are being conducted in Africa.^{4} This lack of interest in considering this region for the roll-out of clinical trials is rooted in lack of knowledge and misconceptions about what can be done.

In the past two decades, funding by development agencies has resulted in the building of important capacity and capabilities in the execution of controlled clinical trials, predominantly focused on infectious diseases, including HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, COVID-19, and Human Papilloma Virus infection. The capacity covers a wide-range of drug and vaccine trials, studies on the accuracy of diagnostic tests, and efficacy and effectiveness of medical devices. A comprehensive database has identified around 5,000 potential clinical research sites throughout Africa.^{5}

## Declining donor funding leaves untapped research capacity

The funding of donor-funded clinical research activities in sub-Saharan Africa has recently declined because of the discontinuation of development aid through several bilateral and multilateral programs. This frees up a large, untapped potential of highly qualified medical professionals trained in Good Clinical Practices (GCP) and working according to Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and policies, and infrastructure related to networks of dedicated clinical research sites, laboratories, and medical equipment. The catchment area of the clinical research sites includes many millions of patients representing an extensive pool of potential study participants.

## Rising burden of non-communicable diseases expands trial potential

Here’s what we can reliably say about that article you linked about an “anti-aging injection” that regrows knee cartilage and prevents arthritis:

📌 What the article is actually reporting

The article you linked is a science news summary of a preclinical research study — not a proven human therapy. It reports that blocking a protein called 15-PGDH helped older mice regenerate knee cartilage and reduced arthritis development after injury in animal models. It also showed some promising results on human knee tissue samples ex vivo (in the lab). ￼

🚫 It is not an approved human treatment yet
   •   There is no FDA-approved injection proven to regrow cartilage in human knees that reliably repairs osteoarthritis. Researchers continue to investigate many potential therapies, but none have yet been validated as a true regeneration cure. ￼
   •   Current clinically used injections (like viscosupplementation/hyaluronic acid, cortisone, or PRP) mainly focus on symptom relief or lubrication, not regenerating real cartilage tissue. ￼
   •   Some experimental approaches (like cell-based therapies, LNA043, or scaffold-based chondrocyte implants) are under research or in early clinical trials but again are not established cures yet. ￼

🧪 Why these kinds of headlines are premature

– Animal models are very useful, but results often don’t translate directly to humans — many promising cartilage regeneration strategies have failed in later human stages. ￼
– News summaries can make early research sound like a “miracle cure,” when in reality it’s an early-stage discovery that may still be years from any real therapy.

📌 Bottom line

The SciTechDaily article is based on legitimate early research, but the claim that this is a current available treatment for people is not true. It’s an exciting scientific step, but no injection so far has been proven to regrow knee cartilage and prevent arthritis in humans as a routine clinical treatment. ￼

# UP and SAACA launch oncology centre for animal treatment and research

Posted on October 13, 2021

The University of Pretoria’s (UP) Faculty of Veterinary Science and the Southern Africa Animal Cancer Association (SAACA) have teamed up to create an oncology centre for clinical cases and research in animals.

At the end of 2020, founder and CEO of SAACA Munnik Marais approached the faculty with a proposal to join forces. Having spent many years fundraising for the Cancer Association of South Africa (CANSA), Marais wanted to create awareness of cancer in animals and encourage treatment and research. To achieve this goal, SAACA was created.

Dr Paolo Pazzi, Section Head of Small Animal Medicine at UP, heads the research aspect of the oncology centre. “The goal of this collaboration is to increase the faculty’s capacity to treat cancer in animals,” he said. “This will result in an increase in research in this field. It will allow for earlier diagnosis of cancer and a wider spectrum of effective treatment options for animals.” 

Dr Anri Celliers and Dr Varaidzo Mukorera, lecturers in Small Animal Internal Medicine, and Professor Gerhard Steenkamp, Section Head of Small Animal Surgery, head up the clinical side of the oncology centre, which is based at the faculty’s Onderstepoort Veterinary Academic Hospital (OVAH). While there are specialist hospitals in South Africa that treat cancer in animals, OVAH is the only one with on-site specialist clinical pathologists/cytologists, and medical and surgical clinicians that work as a team to diagnose and treat cancers. Most patients are cats and dogs with cancer. 

Image

This cat was blind at the point of diagnosis but regained its sight after the first of four radiation treatments. Radiation therapy was performed at the Arcadia unit of Icon Radiotherapy.

“At the faculty, research in the field of oncology includes the investigation of a worm (Spirocerca) that can cause oesophageal cancer in dogs,” Dr Pazzi explained. “The faculty has advanced knowledge in the diagnosis of spirocercosis; the differentiation of benign and malignant spirocercosis; and identification of the surgical predictors of survival for neoplastic spirocercosis.” It can determine whether dogs with cancerous spirocercosis require surgery. “We research which clinical findings or blood work results would give us an indication of success of the surgery and long-term survival after surgery.” 

Ongoing projects in the faculty include the investigation of blood and urine tests that can differentiate between localised cancer and cancer that has spread to other parts of the body. “Our aim at the oncology centre is to focus on common cancers such as mammary cancers as well as various carcinomas and sarcomas,” said Dr Pazzi. “Blood or urine tests will aid in the easier diagnosis and earlier treatment of cancers in animals. Other planned future studies will look at the role that certain blood cells play in the promotion or inhibition of cancer.”

To achieve this, the centre plans to employ more staff, enabling the faculty to accommodate more patients with cancer. “This will allow for increased research into cancer diagnosis and treatment,” Dr Pazzi said. “The clinic currently sees 10 to 30 cancer patients a month, but with the collaboration with SAACA, these numbers are predicted to double.”
